Transforms for Bayesian PCA Imputation

Source: R/mi_pca_transform.R
tf_identity.Rd

Transform obj prior to the Bayesian PCA imputation. Each draw is mapped back to the scale of obj before it is returned.

Usage

tf_identity()

tf_sv(n)

tf_biwhiten(base = tf_identity(), rows = TRUE)

Arguments

n

Integer. The sample size of the squeeze, usually nrow(obj). At least 2.

base

A transform object. The scale the rescaling is applied on: tf_identity(), tf_sv() or a transform of your own, not another tf_biwhiten(). Defaults to tf_identity().

rows

Logical. If TRUE, rescale the rows as well as the columns. Defaults to TRUE.

Value

A transform object, to pass as transform.

Details

The two names. transform = "identity" is tf_identity(), and transform = "logit_biwhiten" is tf_biwhiten(tf_sv(nrow(obj)), rows = TRUE). Build a transform with these functions to change one part of either, such as the logit without the rescaling, or the columns rescaled and the rows not.

tf_identity() fits the values as is.

tf_sv() is for proportions such as DNAm beta values. Each value y is squeezed to (y * (n - 1) + 0.5) / n, which moves 0 and 1 inside the interval (Smithson and Verkuilen, 2006), and then taken to the logit scale. Draws are mapped back and clamped to [0, 1]. Every observed value must lie in [0, 1].

tf_biwhiten() rescales the columns, and with rows = TRUE the rows, of the matrix on the scale of base to a common noise level before the fit, and takes the scales back out of each draw. The scales are estimated once from the observed values, with the column variances shrunk as in Smyth (2004). The rescaling follows the idea of Landa, Zhang and Kluger (2022), with the scales estimated differently.

A transform of your own is a list with name, a string, and two functions, forward(y, ...) and backward(z, ...), where backward() undoes forward() value by value. Both must take ..., since the fit passes them column and row positions. It can be the base of tf_biwhiten().

References

Smithson M, Verkuilen J (2006). A better lemon squeezer? Maximum-likelihood regression with beta-distributed dependent variables. Psychological Methods, 11(1), 54-71. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.11.1.54

Smyth GK (2004). Linear models and empirical Bayes methods for assessing differential expression in microarray experiments. Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology, 3(1), 1-25. doi:10.2202/1544-6115.1027

Landa B, Zhang TTCK, Kluger Y (2022). Biwhitening reveals the rank of a count matrix. SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science, 4(4), 1420-1446. doi:10.1137/21M1456807

See also

mipca(), whose transform argument these build.

Examples

set.seed(1)
sim <- sim_mat(n = 50, p = 20, beta = TRUE)
obj <- sim$input

# The same model as transform = "logit_biwhiten"
tf_logit_biwhiten <- tf_biwhiten(tf_sv(nrow(obj)), rows = TRUE)

# The logit without the rescaling
tf_logit <- tf_sv(nrow(obj))

# The columns rescaled, the rows not
tf_cols <- tf_biwhiten(tf_sv(nrow(obj)), rows = FALSE)
fit <- mipca(obj, rank = 2, transform = tf_cols, seed = 1)
fit
#> si_mi fit: 50 x 20, 100 imputed cells, 400 draws
#>   next: as.matrix() with 'draw' for a completed matrix, summary() for Rhat and ESS
